content: At the facility level, the data excludes individuals who transferred out within 12 months, those who have died, those who are known to have discontinued antiretroviral therapy (ART), and those lost to follow-up. Lost to Follow-Up (LFU): This refers to patients who have not attended their scheduled appointments for three months or more (90 days or longer). Stopped ART: Patients who discontinue their antiretroviral regimen for various reasons are categorized accordingly. There may be overlap between the LFU and stopped ART categories, as patients who stop treatment without notifying clinic staff are classified as LFU. The Three Interlinked Patient Monitoring Systems (3IPMS) for HIV care/ART, maternal and child health (MCH)/prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT), and TB/HIV use a standardized minimum data set and illustrative tools. Reasons for stopping ART, as coded in the 3IPMS, include drug toxicity or side effects, adverse drug reactions, pregnancy, treatment failure, poor adherence, illness, hospitalization, drug stock-outs, financial constraints, patient decisions, planned interruptions, and the end of the MTCT risk period in countries using Option B for PMTCT. Measuring ART Adherence Adherence is critical for successful treatment outcomes and minimizing HIV drug resistance (HIVDR). When viral load testing is not routinely available, viral suppression can be assessed in a representative sample of ART patients using an HIVDR survey. While these methods do not confirm whether patients take the drugs as prescribed, drug pick-up has been associated with viral suppression. Early warning indicators (EWIs) are used to prevent HIV drug resistance, with good performance defined as >90% adherence and passable performance as >80%. High retention rates are a key indicator of program success and quality. Programs with low retention rates should investigate barriers such as drug stock-outs, inappropriate regimens, or access issues. Programs should also monitor ART survival rates, which reflect the percentage of patients alive at specific time points after ART initiation. Pediatric and Adolescent HIV Care The care and treatment needs of children and adolescents vary by age. Early ART initiation is a priority for infants and children under five, as all are eligible for treatment. Adolescents, however, often experience higher attrition and mortality rates. Monitoring systems must track children through the HIV care cascade as they transition from infancy to adulthood, ensuring continuity of care. Age-disaggregated data is essential to identify gaps in service delivery and inform program planning.g., 3, 6, 9 months) also considered to identify retention issues. Disaggregating ART coverage and retention indicators by key populations helps assess equity in service delivery. HIV and Co-Infections The 2013 WHO guidelines recommend that people living with HIV who are co-infected with active tuberculosis (TB) or hepatitis B with severe chronic liver disease should start ART regardless of CD4 count. Challenges in Pediatric HIV Monitoring Tracking children through the care cascade is challenging due to multiple service points and frequent transfers between facilities. Unique patient identifiers and computerized systems can improve data linkage and reduce gaps in care. Age-disaggregated data is particularly important for monitoring ART initiation and retention among children and adolescents, as their needs and barriers to care differ significantly from adults. Strategic Information and Program Improvement Programs should use age-disaggregated indicators to monitor progress in identifying, enrolling, and retaining children and adolescents in care. If coverage rates are low, programs should assess HIV diagnosis strategies and barriers to care. Quality-of-care indicators can help evaluate the effectiveness of interventions and identify areas for improvement, such as early diagnosis and retention in care. Conclusion High-quality ART management, including early initiation, adherence, and retention, directly increases the likelihood of viral suppression and reduces the risk of drug resistance.
